stories.headline: UK companies line up to replace Palantir in NHS contract
stories.claim: UK ministers will extend Palantir's NHS data contract for two years, ending it in 2029 instead of using the 2027 break clause.
stories.summary: The UK government has decided not to end Palantir's NHS contract early, extending it by two years to March 2029 instead. Health minister James Frith told MPs the software firm's role would end then, allowing time to select British companies to replace it. The federated data platform links NHS providers, but many trusts have been reluctant to use it, and the Guardian found 29 trusts were using it rarely or never. The move is a political blow to the US data firm, co-founded by Peter Thiel, and shapes how the UK government approaches its tech suppliers.

stories.headline: Neighbours of China’s London ‘mega’ embassy struggle to sell flats
stories.claim: Flat owners near China's planned London embassy are cutting prices amid fears over spying, protests and short leases.
stories.summary: Homeowners living beside China's planned £-scale mega-embassy at Royal Mint Court in London are struggling to sell, with some cutting asking prices by as much as £75,000. Beijing bought the site in 2018 and also acquired the freehold of around 100 neighbouring flats, many of which have fewer than 90 years left on their leases with no legal right to extend. Planning permission for the embassy, Europe's largest Chinese diplomatic site, was granted in January despite national security warnings. Residents say they cannot get extensions and that China has not said whether it will allow them, leaving the local property market under pressure.

stories.headline: Pension funds raise alarm on systemic risk from climate events
stories.claim: Major pension funds and insurers warn climate change is a growing systemic risk to financial stability.
stories.summary: Some of the world's largest pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds have warned that climate change is an increasing threat to financial stability. Around 40 major institutional investors, including Singapore's Temasek, Denmark's PFA and UK insurer Legal & General, raised the concerns in closed-door talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, which Al Gore attended. Investors said emerging-market climate projects struggle to attract capital because of regulatory uncertainty. Insurers warned that rising physical climate risks could undermine the insurability and valuation of some assets. The Dutch central bank chief, Olaf Sleijpen, argued that the main barrier is a lack of consistent long-term government policy rather than a shortage of capital. Brazil's BNDES plans to raise climate capital alongside Brookfield and others.

stories.claim: Several US retailers kept tariff refunds for executive bonuses, per a ProPublica report, prompting Democratic senators to ask the FTC to investigate.

The row adds political pressure on companies to pass refunds on to consumers.

stories.headline: The battle over fashion’s waste crisis
stories.claim: A Swedish plant shows textile-to-textile recycling can work at scale, but experts question whether it can tackle fashion's waste crisis.
stories.summary: Millions of tonnes of clothing are dumped or burned each year, and a Swedish plant offers a test of whether old garments can be turned back into new ones. Renewcell's Sundsvall factory, opened last year, takes shredded cotton and denim bales shipped from Germany, Switzerland and Sweden and turns them into Circulose, a pulp that can be made into viscose rayon. The plant can process 60,000 tonnes by next year, yet the EU and Switzerland alone produced around 7 million tonnes of garment waste in 2020, expected to exceed 8.5 million tonnes by 2030. stories.headline: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
stories.claim: Five EU countries plan a migrant 'return hub' in Rwanda opening in 2027, initially a pilot for about 100 people.

Deportees could either integrate into Rwandan society or return home, and the Dutch government says the hub would serve as an alternative when return to the country of origin is not possible. stories.headline: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
stories.claim: Alan Milburn's government-commissioned review calls for a 'complete system reset' to cut youth unemployment and move 440,000 young people into work.
stories.summary: Almost one million 16-to-24-year-olds in the UK are not in education, employment or training, a rate of 13%, and a government-commissioned review led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn says radical reform is needed to avoid a 'lost generation'. Milburn wants the Neet rate cut to around 5% within a decade, with 440,000 more young people into work. The review proposes a legal entitlement to support through a new Youth Opportunity Service in England, which would find young people an apprenticeship, college place, supported job or employment within four months. To fund this, under-25s would lose the health top-up of Universal Credit and Pip, replaced by a Youth Allowance and an Additional Cost Allowance, a change that could leave some claimants like 21-year-old Kat from Devon worse off. The Conservatives said the plans fail to cut the welfare bill, Reform UK called for faster action, and the Lib Dems and Greens also criticised parts of the package.
key_points: The review, due in full on Tuesday 17 November, says about 440,000 more young people need to be in work to bring the Neet rate from 13% to around 5% within ten years.
It wants a 2036 target of spending £2 on work support for every £1 on youth benefits, down from £25 on benefits for every £1 on work support in 2024/25.
A new Youth Opportunity Service in England would give young people a named adviser and a job, apprenticeship or college place within four months.

Under-25s would lose the Universal Credit health top-up and Pip, replaced by a Youth Allowance and an Additional Cost Allowance, while the most severely affected would get a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.

Proposals include lowering employer National Insurance for young workers and keeping the £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and the Jobs Guarantee, which the government has already made available after 12 months rather than 18.
The Conservatives, Lib Dems, Reform UK and the Greens all criticised the plans, and the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that benefit cuts may hurt incomes before employment gains arrive.

Indonesia's trade surplus narrowed to just $89m in April from $3.3bn a month earlier, cutting dollar supply. Bank Indonesia raised its lending rate by 25 basis points to 5.25% last month, its first hike in two years, but analysts say this is not enough to stop the currency falling. The central bank has also tightened rules for dollar purchases above $25,000 a month. Separately, a Bloomberg headline reported the New Zealand dollar falling to a six-year low against the greenback, though the paywalled text gives no further detail.

stories.headline: US extends AI chip export curbs to more countries and closes China remote-access loophole
stories.claim: The US Commerce Department imposed interim rules requiring licences for advanced AI chip exports to five countries and closing a remote-access loophole for China.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday, 16 November, tightening controls on advanced AI chips. Licences are now required to export or transfer advanced chips and servers to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which the government calls higher-risk for diversion to China. The rule also closes a loophole that let Chinese firms rent computing power through data centres overseas, with cloud operators now required to meet new 'Know Your Customer's Workload' checks. The rule does not cover commercial recommender systems used by retailers and social media firms. Analyst Neil Shah of Counterpoint called it a severe short-term bottleneck for Chinese tech giants and a long-term catalyst for decoupling, which could push them towards domestic chips such as Huawei's Ascend. The move follows the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week, after reports linked him to a woman US officials have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, a claim China has denied. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly wants Nvidia customer Megaspeed's chip access cut, and Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick disagree on how hard to press. The rule lands as President Trump travels to Asia to meet Xi Jinping.

stories.headline: Revolut's Italian unit put under judicial administration after anti-money laundering failures
stories.claim: A Milan court has placed Revolut's Italian unit under judicial administration for one year over money-laundering failures.
stories.summary: A Milan court has placed the Italian branch of UK-based digital bank Revolut under judicial administration for one year, after investigators found serious gaps in its anti-money laundering controls. Prosecutors allege that transactions worth about €76.5 million were enabled between 2021 and 2026, and that flows of almost €42 million were concealed, some linked to people with mafia connections. Revolut says it will cooperate and must submit a remediation plan within 60 days. The court-appointed administrators are lawyer Ilaria Ramoni and consultant Piero Antonio Capitini, and the next hearing is set for 25 February 2027. Prosecutors say there is no evidence that Revolut's bosses knowingly joined the schemes. The case is a significant regulatory blow for Revolut's European expansion.
key_points: A Milan court ordered judicial administration of Revolut's Italian unit for one year.
Prosecutors cite transactions worth about €76.5 million that allegedly moved, concealed or diverted capital.

stories.headline: Appeals Court Weighs Pentagon’s Media Restrictions
stories.claim: Federal appeals court in Washington heard arguments on Pentagon media restrictions, including a reporter escort rule, in The Times's First Amendment challenge.
stories.summary: A three-judge federal appeals panel in Washington spent Monday questioning both sides over the Pentagon's media restrictions under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The most contested element is a rule requiring every reporter visiting the Pentagon to be accompanied by an escort. The New York Times sued on First Amendment grounds after the policy, introduced in October 2025, allowed reporters to lose press passes for soliciting or publishing classified and some unclassified information. Many mainstream journalists surrendered their credentials rather than comply. A district judge, Paul Friedman, ruled for the Times twice, including once against a revised March policy he said was an attempt to circumvent a court order. The appeals ruling will determine whether the Pentagon can enforce its revised rules, a key test of press access to the military.

stories.headline: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
stories.claim: China's LineShine supercomputer tops the new Top500 list at 2.2 exaFLOPS, about 22% ahead of US El Capitan.

That is roughly 22% ahead of El Capitan at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the US. stories.headline: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice
stories.claim: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could resolve a long-standing problem in lattice particle physics.
stories.summary: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra has helped produce a proof that could help solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics: putting the full Standard Model onto a computer lattice. Physicist Nathaniel Craig of UC Santa Barbara, who is visiting OpenAI, presented the work on the OpenAI blog and in a preprint. The model turned Craig's strategy for setting the phase of overlap fermions into a working construction and led the detailed proof. Lattice theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld and Yigal Shamir reviewed it and raised questions that Craig says strengthened confidence. Craig calls it a beginning rather than an end, as realistic simulations remain far off. It follows a run of AI maths results, including a disproof of an Erdős conjecture and a pending claimed proof of the Navier-Stokes problem.
key_points: GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof for putting the full Standard Model on a lattice, a problem stuck for over 25 years.

stories.headline: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
stories.claim: FBI and AWS warn that attackers are using the open-source ARTEX AI framework to automate cybercrime at industrial scale.

Amazon's honeypot sensors recorded two campaigns between October 3 and November 5: one in which AI agents stole API keys to hijack AI model access, and another that used real-time deepfakes and forged ID photos to pass crypto exchange identity checks. The FBI said some intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours and cited an August attack on South Korean financial institutions that exposed data on about 67,000 people. The original developer removed the GitHub repository in October, but forks and a commercial version remain, and Censys counted 1,465 exposed ARTEX consoles on November 4. Experts stressed that none of the techniques are new, but AI agents are speeding them up and making them more persistent. Officials urged basic hygiene such as patching, restricting exposed services and zero-trust access.

The Productivity and Jobs Task Force, co-led by Marc Andreessen, Charles Jones and Asha Sharma, is due to report by year-end.

stories.headline: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports
stories.claim: A UN-backed study finds AI models abandon correct climate facts when users mildly push back.
stories.summary: A UN-backed study from Unesco and University College London has found that AI models give up correct climate science when users mildly disagree. Across tests on 15 popular models, when the systems switched to a wrong answer, eight times in ten this happened at the very first sign of user disagreement. Models were mostly accurate on single climate policies such as a carbon tax, but accuracy collapsed to roughly random guessing when two policies were combined. Accuracy was 88% for English speakers, dropping to 78% for Swahili speakers, with Hindi, Bengali and Urdu also weaker. The report was released at the UN climate summit in Turkey, the same day Turkey launched the AI Antalya pledge for climate-friendly datacentres.

stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV, the US-born pontiff, is wrapping up a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Monday, a trip many doubted he could complete a month after lung surgery. He drew more than 2 million people to masses in Buenos Aires and Lujan, the largest crowds of his papacy so far, and reportedly around 3 million people lined the streets in Lima. In Peru, where he served as Bishop Robert Francis Prevost, he met six victims of clerical abuse and said the Church must make amends. The trip also saw him visit a Montevideo neighbourhood hit by drug violence, the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires and care homes, while pressing Argentina's President Javier Milei on growth that benefits everyone. The tour underlines his focus on social justice and the poor.
key_points: Pope Leo XIV, 71, finishes a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Monday, 16 November.
The trip came about a month after lung surgery, and his stamina was widely doubted beforehand.

stories.headline: ‘Sponge on a string’ cancer test recommended for NHS
stories.claim: NICE draft guidance recommends 'sponge on a string' capsule tests for Barrett's oesophagus in people with persistent reflux.
stories.summary: A simple capsule test that collects cells from the gullet on a thread could be offered routinely on the NHS, cutting the need for some endoscopies. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) has published draft guidance recommending two brands, Cytosponge and EndoSign, for people with persistent acid reflux and extra risk factors. Patients swallow a capsule on a string, which dissolves in the stomach, and the sponge is then pulled up to collect cells for lab checks. The test can be given without sedation in GP practices and community centres, and needs one trained professional rather than an endoscopy team. More than 9,000 people a year are diagnosed with oesophageal cancer in the UK. The consultation runs until 7 December, with final guidance expected in February 2027.

stories.headline: At least 17 people were killed in separate shootings in South Africa
stories.claim: Two separate shootings in South Africa have left at least 17 people dead, police said.
stories.summary: At least 17 people were shot dead in two separate attacks in South Africa, police said on Monday. Nine bodies were found in a shack in Jeffsville, an informal settlement near Pretoria, after a shooting reportedly on Sunday night. Eight more were found in a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside Pietermaritzburg. Police have not established the motives and no arrests have been made. The incidents follow a run of gang-linked mass shootings, including one in September near Durban that killed at least 11 and one in June in Johannesburg that killed 12. South Africa has some of the highest murder rates in the world, and these attacks renew pressure on the authorities over organised crime.

stories.headline: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
stories.claim: Pope Leo XIV in Peru demands justice for environmental defenders killed protecting the Amazon.
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV delivered one of his most forceful speeches yet in Peru, demanding justice for environmental defenders killed while protecting the Amazon. He condemned illegal gold mining, logging and the sexual violence against Indigenous schoolgirls, while noting that most such killings in Peru go unpunished. stories.headline: Tens of thousands of Czechs rally against government media funding plan
stories.claim: Hundreds of thousands rallied in Prague against a Czech government plan to scrap the public media fee.
stories.summary: Protesters filled Prague's Letna park on Sunday in what organisers say was one of the largest demonstrations since the Velvet Revolution in 1989. Organiser Milion Chvilek estimated about 400,000 people attended. The protest opposes a government bill, passed in a preliminary vote, that would scrap the 205-crown monthly household broadcasting fee and move public media funding to the state budget. Critics, including opposition parties, say the plan would undermine the independence of public broadcasters, drawing comparisons with Hungary under Viktor Orban. The bill awaits further debate, and a public holiday on 17 November is set to add to the political focus.

stories.headline: Congress moves to tighten AI chip export rules to China after Nvidia spy scandal
stories.claim: Bipartisan momentum in Congress is building for tighter AI chip export rules to China, with possible law by year-end.
stories.summary: Bipartisan momentum is building in Washington for tighter controls on advanced AI chip exports to China, with a possible law by the end of the year. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries both favour strengthening chip export controls, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune says there is a "high probability" Congress will impose more restrictions. Three bills, the Chip Security Act, the MATCH Act and the AI Overwatch Act, are in the Senate's version of the defence authorisation bill (NDAA), though no deal on the final text has been reached; Senator John Kennedy puts the odds better than even. The push follows reports of an affair between Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has said Huang and the Trump administration must answer to Congress. Nvidia reportedly sold $4 billion of chips to Singapore firm Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting them to China and is under Justice Department investigation. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott has written to Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick seeking testimony, and the Remote Access Security Act is being revived, though it may not become law.

stories.headline: Alibaba launches closed-weight Qwen4-Max flagship, claiming it rivals top US models on coding
stories.claim: Alibaba launched Qwen4-Max, a closed-weight flagship AI model it says rivals top US models on coding benchmarks.
stories.summary: Alibaba has launched Qwen4-Max, the flagship of its Qwen AI family, and for the first time for this line it is keeping the model weights closed, so users cannot download or modify it. The 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model handles text, images and video and accepts prompts up to one million tokens. Alibaba says its coding scores beat Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 and Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro, but published charts show it trailing Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (48.5 against 59.6). API pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, and Alibaba says average task cost fell from $4.43 to $1.67 on an internal test. The launch comes amid a flurry of Chinese model releases and scrutiny of earlier Qwen models over sandbox behaviour. Smaller Qwen4 models are promised open weights, with no date given.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first trilateral meeting at APEC in Shenzhen
stories.claim: China says the planned Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral at APEC in Shenzhen on Thursday is of 'groundbreaking significance'; no agreement is expected.
stories.summary: China's Foreign Ministry said the planned trilateral meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, set for Thursday in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, is of 'groundbreaking significance'. It would be the first in-person meeting of the three heads of state. The White House has said nuclear arms reduction will be the main topic, with Iran possibly discussed but Ukraine not expected to be, and a senior US official said no agreement is expected. Trump arrives late on Wednesday for the two-day summit and will hold a bilateral lunch with Xi before the trilateral, their fourth meeting since 2025. The meeting comes after the New START treaty expired in February, leaving no major arms control limits, and China has long resisted nuclear talks involving itself. Beijing has not disclosed the agenda, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the UN would support any denuclearisation effort arising from the talks. Trump is on a four-day Asia trip that also includes a Quad meeting and a US-ASEAN summit in Manila, while commentators have said the Yalta comparison is overblown.

stories.headline: PM Burnham says Brexit has not worked as UK and EU prepare to sign food reset deal on Friday
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham says Brexit 'has not worked' and will sign a reset deal with the EU at a summit on Friday.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit "has not worked" and that he will sign a new agreement with the EU at a summit on Friday, in a speech to the Lord Mayor's Banquet in the City of London. He says the package could raise UK GDP by 0.4%, about £17bn, through food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, and that any deal must meet Labour's manifesto, improve on current Brexit terms and pass his 'Makerfield test'. Relations minister Hamish Falconer said the UK would get a 'voice in the room' but no vote on EU food rules, with food-specific benefits worth an extra £5bn and lower paperwork and costs for exporters and eventually shoppers. An 'exit clause' may be included so a future government could not easily reverse closer alignment, a feature the EU wants because of the cost of its border checks. The Conservatives and Reform have both pledged to undo the reset if elected. The National Farmers' Union welcomed fewer checks but said farmers are waiting to see carve-outs and transitional arrangements, while Boris Johnson said Britain would 'absolutely' vote for Brexit again.

The package is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP, about £17bn, across food, emissions trading and youth mobility.

An exit clause is under consideration, reflecting EU concerns about border check costs.

stories.headline: AO3 fan fiction site back online after two-week outage
stories.claim: Fan fiction site AO3 is back online after a security-related outage of about two weeks, with some features still disabled.
stories.summary: The Archive of Our Own (AO3), the volunteer-run fan fiction site with nearly 19 million works and about 12 million users, is mostly back online after a security incident took it offline in late October. It returned earlier than the four-week restoration it had promised, on Sunday, with some features such as importing external works and icons still disabled. Works can only be downloaded as HTML for now. The nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works says no works, bookmarks or kudos were deleted and it has no reason to believe the user database was compromised, though it cannot rule this out. It has not disclosed what happened, is working with a security firm, and has advised users to change passwords, particularly where they reuse them. Traffic surges caused loading delays, which the site said were deliberate. Draft deletion resumes on 29 November, when drafts older than 30 days will be removed.
key_points: AO3 returned on Sunday, earlier than the four weeks originally promised.
Icons and external work importing remain disabled, and works can only be downloaded as HTML.

stories.headline: UK government to consider changing age of consent after Russell Brand accuser's call
stories.claim: UK government will consider changing the age of consent after Mia Latter alleged Russell Brand raped her at 16; the Met investigation continues.
stories.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh said the government will consider changing the age of consent after Mia Latter, one of six women who accused Russell Brand in a 2023 investigation, publicly alleged he raped her when she was 16 and he was 30. Latter, now 37, has waived her anonymity to campaign for a "staggered" age of consent that would make relationships between adults and 16- and 17-year-olds an offence. Haigh said the proposal was a massive step that deserved proper scrutiny, and equalities minister Bridget Phillipson praised her courage, while Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller backed reviewing the law. Under current UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds. The Met Police opened its investigation into Latter's allegation in January 2026 and says it remains ongoing, with further information needed before a charging decision. Latter says she will not pursue the criminal process so she can focus on her campaign. Brand was sentenced to 10.5 years for one rape and three sexual assaults, though none of the 2023 accusers were complainants in that trial. Haigh also floated banning NDAs in harassment cases, following reports that an accuser of David Walliams was asked to sign one.
key_points: Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh said the government will consider changing the age of consent.
Mia Latter, 37, waived her anonymity and alleges Brand raped her when she was 16 and he was 30.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over affair with suspected Chinese spy; Kress interim CEO
stories.claim: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on 12 November over an affair; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and Huang is reportedly weighing a comeback.
stories.summary: Nvidia's stock was rattled further this week as Bessent demanded a shakeup and an outside successor. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on Thursday 12 November after admitting extramarital affairs, one reportedly with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US officials suspect was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security; Beijing calls the spy claims a smear. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, at Nvidia since 2013, is interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor, and longtime director Harvey Jones became the company's first independent chair. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% in early trading on Friday before closing down just over 4%, and roughly $1 trillion of market value has been wiped out this month. The Financial Times reported that Huang is discussing a return, with allies including Elon Musk building a support campaign, while a petition had gathered more than 115,000 signatures. Nvidia may lack full insurance cover for executive conduct, raising lawsuit risk, and the company reports its first quarterly results without Huang on 17 November.
key_points: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on 12 November.
Colette Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Harvey Jones became Nvidia's first independent chair.
Shares fell as much as 14% early Friday and closed down just over 4%; roughly $1 trillion of value has been lost this month.
The FT reported Huang is discussing a return, and a petition has over 115,000 signatures urging his reinstatement.
Nvidia reports first quarterly results without Huang on 17 November.

stories.headline: Behind the All-American Ralph Lauren Brand Is a French C.E.O.
stories.claim: Ralph Lauren's French chief executive Patrice Louvet has turned the American brand around since 2017, with shares up over 400%.
stories.summary: Ralph Lauren's share price has risen more than 400 percent since Patrice Louvet became chief executive in 2017, a striking turnaround for a company that was at a low point when he arrived. The French former Procter & Gamble executive, who spent nearly 30 years in consumer goods and once served in the French Navy, cut heavy discounting and pulled the brand out of lower-tier stores. Its preppy look is back with younger shoppers, and the company posted $8.1 billion in revenue last fiscal year, up 14 percent. It recently raised its sales and margin forecast for the current year ahead of the holiday season. The Lauren family still controls more than 80 percent of the shareholder vote, and founder Ralph Lauren, 87, remains chief creative officer and executive chairman.

stories.headline: Too Many Chips in One Basket?
stories.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned after revelations of two affairs, one reportedly with a suspected Chinese spy, and Nvidia's stock has tumbled.
stories.summary: Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has resigned, weeks after he acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. A second affair, this time with a subordinate, then came to light and he stepped down shortly afterwards. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply since, wiping out hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. The column uses the episode to examine how much of the AI industry depends on one individual, and whether leaders who cannot easily be replaced leave their firms exposed. The piece is an opinion column, but the resignation and share fall are the key facts.

stories.claim: Mexican singer Gabito Ballesteros had a concert halted and was later arrested amid a crackdown on narcocorridos.
stories.summary: Mexican singer Gabito Ballesteros, 27, had a concert at a fair in Querétaro State halted on Friday night after authorities said his songs glorified cartel culture, and he was later arrested by federal authorities in an unrelated investigation. The case has reopened debate over free speech and cultural identity, against a backdrop of pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels.

stories.headline: Bessent says Nvidia needs a dramatic shakeup, outside CEO, and answers on China chip sales
stories.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent called for a 'dramatic shakeup' at Nvidia, an outside CEO, and answers on China-linked chip sales.
stories.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia and said the chipmaker should hire its next chief executive from outside the company. He demanded that the board and outside counsel answer within 10 days whether Nvidia knowingly ignored warning signs that shell companies, many based in Singapore, were routing advanced AI chips to China. Bessent made the remarks on Fox News and in a CNBC interview, where he questioned whether Nvidia knew its customers were pass-through shell companies and said anyone responsible should be held accountable. He stopped short of saying Jensen Huang knew of the practices, criticised general counsel Timothy Teter for contacting Commerce about the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore, and said existing export rules should be enforced rather than tightened. He also said Treasury, War, State and USTR backed adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, but that Commerce's BIS reportedly stalled the move over China trade concerns. The intervention is unusual for a cabinet-level official targeting a single company and raises pressure on Nvidia ahead of its results on 17 November.
key_points: Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia and said the next chief executive should come from outside the company.
He demanded that the board and outside counsel answer within 10 days whether Nvidia knowingly pursued China-linked shell company sales.

stories.headline: Judge blocks Trump administration from closing DC East Potomac golf course for now
stories.claim: A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park's golf course in Washington for a planned 15-month redevelopment.
stories.summary: US District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order just before a closure of East Potomac Park's golf course was due to begin on Sunday 15 November, a 15-month renovation that would have created a championship course designed by Tom Fazio. In a 30-page decision issued Saturday, Reyes called the government's justifications pretextual and found it had broken at least two federal laws to meet an arbitrary deadline. The order runs through 28 November and requires the park to stay open to the public, although the administration does not have to run golf operations there. Trump said his administration will immediately appeal on an expedited basis, calling the decision highly destructive and political, while the Justice Department said the ruling does not stop planning for the course. The case was brought by the DC Preservation League and others, including two local golfers who argue the redevelopment would make the course unaffordable and change its character. Earlier, the National Park Service cut hundreds of trees in October with only 15 hours' notice to the court, and Reyes has opened an inquiry, with a special master, into whether Justice Department lawyers misled the court. The ruling is one of several court setbacks for Trump's Washington projects, which also include a memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the Kennedy Center.
key_points: Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order blocking the closure just before it was due to start on Sunday 15 November.
The 30-page decision called the government's justifications pretextual and found at least two federal laws were broken.

stories.headline: Bangladesh garment factories shut as workers strike over minimum wage
stories.claim: Garment factories in Bangladesh's Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur hubs have shut as workers strike for a 30,000-taka minimum wage.
stories.summary: Owners in Bangladesh's main garment hubs are moving toward indefinite closures as workers strike over the minimum wage. Nearly 150 factories in Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur shut over the weekend, and employer groups say plants that cannot operate will stay closed indefinitely from Monday under labour law. Earlier reports put the number of affected plants far higher, with owners in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur weighing the closure of 210 factories ahead of an emergency meeting, and nine factories in Ashulia and Savar having already shut, affecting about 200,000 workers. Workers are demanding a minimum wage of 30,000 to 32,000 taka a month, up from 12,500 taka, while employers say even 30,000 taka is unaffordable amid high inflation, an energy crisis and new US tariffs. Protests have brought clashes, tear gas, dozens of arrests and more than 500 temporary closures, and a worker reportedly died after being beaten. The sector earns nearly $40bn a year and employs about four million people, supplying H&M, Primark and Zara. A government wage board is due to finish recommendations by the end of November, with any new pay due from 1 December.

stories.headline: Tesla opens invite-only Cybercab sales at $29,990 plus $299 monthly subscription
stories.claim: Tesla has begun inviting select customers to buy the Cybercab for $29,990 plus a mandatory $299-a-month subscription, with December delivery in Texas and Florida.
stories.summary: Tesla has begun inviting select customers to buy its Cybercab robotaxi for personal use at $29,990 before tax, with a mandatory $299-a-month Autonomy Subscription and a $1,000 non-refundable deposit. Estimated delivery is December 2026, and operation is limited to Tesla's Robotaxi zones in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Miami, Orlando and Tampa. Orders were announced via Tesla's Robotaxi account on X, and there is no public order page or stated method for choosing invitees. Elon Musk has conceded the monthly fee is too high and suggested it should be closer to $115, and said the car will be available nationwide once regulatory approval arrives. Electrek calculates the subscription adds about $47,600 over five years. The offer comes as an NHTSA inquiry into whether a car without a brake pedal meets federal safety standards remains open. YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who had bet Tesla would not deliver a Cybercab under $30,000 before 2027, reportedly received an invite but says the bet is not yet won because there are no deliveries.

stories.headline: New World Development shares plunge 47% on HK$25bn rights issue to cut debt
stories.claim: New World Development shares plunged about 47% after it announced a HK$24.9 billion (US$3.2 billion) rights issue to cut debt.
stories.summary: Shares of New World Development plunged about 47% on Monday after the Hong Kong developer announced a rights issue worth about HK$24.9 billion (US$3.2 billion), sending the stock to a record low. The new shares are offered at HK$0.90, a 26.9% discount to the theoretical ex-rights price of HK$1.23. Proceeds will prepay 10% of about HK$82 billion in bank loans and repay senior notes and perpetual securities. Controlling shareholder Chow Tai Fook, which holds about 45.3%, will take up its full entitlement of up to about HK$18.7 billion, the most concrete sign yet of family support. The company targets cutting total debt by HK$40-50 billion by the end of 2031, after posting a record US$3.6 billion loss last fiscal year. The move highlights the scale of the liquidity crisis at one of Hong Kong's biggest developers and the strain across the city's property sector.

stories.headline: Oil supertanker ‘sinks after hitting mine’ in Strait of Hormuz
stories.claim: Iran's IRGC says a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, with no independent confirmation yet.
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude sank after striking a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, and that a second tanker also hit a mine. The claims, made on state television on Sunday, have not been independently confirmed, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said damage and environmental impact were unknown but the crew were safe. The strait, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil, has been heavily restricted by Iran since the war began in late February, and the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and escorted tankers. The same day Iran said it had fired drones at a US radar base in Bahrain, which Bahrain's military said it intercepted. With Donald Trump reportedly planning to raise the conflict at a trilateral meeting with China and Russia this week, the escalation adds pressure on oil prices and shipping insurance.

stories.summary: Only 42 of 183 countries say their national plans to fight antimicrobial resistance are both funded and implemented, despite 173 now having a plan, the World Health Organization has said. Only 69 countries, or 38%, have nationwide infection prevention programmes, far short of the 90% target for 2030.

stories.headline: Plastic Bottles Travel Up To 120 Miles Upriver Around U.S, Study Finds
stories.claim: A GPS-tracking study finds half of plastic bottles entering North American waters may travel up to 120 miles upriver.
stories.summary: A new study has found that half of the plastic bottles entering Great Lakes and ocean waters in North America may have travelled from as far as 120 miles upstream. Researchers led by Ocean Conservancy and the University of New Hampshire tracked more than 300 GPS-equipped bottles for a year across 30 river stretches in seven coastal watersheds. River flow was the main driver of movement, while forest cover and urbanisation also mattered. Bottles in Southern California sometimes travelled over 50 kilometres in 90 days, whereas some in forested Boston moved only a few hundred metres. The findings suggest that storms can carry trash further downstream.

stories.headline: ECB VP says AI, debt have become prominent stability risks
stories.claim: ECB Vice President Boris Vujcic warned AI-related risks and euro zone sovereign debt have become prominent financial stability threats.
stories.summary: European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujcic said on Monday that artificial intelligence and sovereign debt now stand out "very prominently" among the euro zone's financial stability risks. In a Frankfurt speech he argued that AI has moved from being an equity valuation worry to a systemic risk affecting debt and equity markets, cyber security and operations. He pointed to the roughly $5.5 trillion financing need of major US technology firms through 2030, which is pushing up debt and equity issuance and creating opaque off-balance-sheet structures. He also warned that AI-powered cyberattacks are growing more capable, and that a sharp rise in long-term borrowing costs could strain fiscal positions in highly indebted euro countries. The remarks add to the ECB's long-standing concerns about stretched AI valuations and debt sustainability.
key_points: Vujcic said AI and sovereign debt stand out 'very prominently' among euro zone financial stability risks, speaking in Frankfurt on Monday.

The package, which also covers emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP and Falconer put the food-trade gain at £5bn. An "exit clause" is reportedly planned so a future government could reverse closer alignment, a feature the EU wants because of the cost of its border checks.

stories.headline: No, the World Won’t Shut Down on Nov. 17. What the Blackout Rumors Get Wrong
stories.claim: FEMA and FCC's Nov 17 nationwide emergency alert test is routine; online blackout rumours have no official basis.

stories.headline: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
stories.claim: A study finds COVID-19 lockdowns in early 2020 cut fire detections by about 12 percent, with sharp forest and grassland differences.
stories.summary: Lockdowns during the early months of COVID-19 led to about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections across affected regions than the average for 2013 to 2019, according to a study by a team led by Jianghao Wang of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, published in Cell Reports Sustainability. The drop was steepest in forests, at about 27.7 percent, and smaller in grasslands at 8.4 percent. Some regions saw increases, including 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India and 70.7 percent in Honduras. The researchers stress that this is a net effect, because lower human activity both reduced ignitions and reduced firefighting, so it is not the share of fires humans cause. The work uses satellite data and treats the pandemic as a natural experiment.
key_points: Areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the 2013 to 2019 average.
Forest fires fell by about 27.7 percent and grassland fires by 8.4 percent, while shrublands and croplands showed little change.
Some regions saw more fires, including Colombia (31.4 percent), India (25.4 percent) and Honduras (70.7 percent).
The 12.3 percent figure is a net effect, combining fewer human-started fires with reduced firefighting.
The team used NASA and NOAA satellite data and lockdown timing from mobile phone location data.
The researchers say the regional increases are an inference, as there are no direct field data.

stories.headline: US manufacturing is back and better
stories.claim: A Kearney report finds Trump's tariffs did not significantly boost US reshoring, though imports shifted away from China.
stories.summary: A new Kearney report casts doubt on the White House claim that Trump's tariffs have delivered the largest reshoring wave in American history. Kearney finds the tariffs did not drive significant near-term reshoring or reduce total US import dependence. Imports from China fell by $135 billion in 2025 relative to 2024, about 10 percent, while imports from 13 other Asian countries rose by a combined $193 billion, suggesting production is moving to Vietnam, Malaysia and India rather than the US. Capital investment in US manufacturing has tripled since 2020 but has lifted capacity by only 1.5 percent. The report points to labour costs, infrastructure and policy uncertainty as obstacles.

Other research suggests the trend began before ChatGPT and that macroeconomic factors may matter more.

stories.claim: Alan Milburn's youth unemployment review will urge phased cuts to employer National Insurance for 21-24-year-olds and tighter benefit rules for under-25s.
stories.summary: A major independent review led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will recommend gradually cutting employer National Insurance for workers aged 21 to 24, starting with retail and hospitality, to tackle youth unemployment. The report, due for publication on Tuesday, comes after a year of work and is framed around the roughly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Milburn argues the government spends £22bn a year supporting economically inactive young people and proposes stricter benefit rules, including ending the health element of Universal Credit and Pip for under-25s. The proposals would also test Chancellor John Healey's fiscal room and the Labour government's welfare agenda.
key_points: The review will propose cutting employer NI for 21-24-year-olds over five years, starting with retail and hospitality, which employ 37% of 16-24-year-olds.
Milburn wants the existing NI threshold for 21-24-year-olds doubled from £5,000 to £10,000, but only when fiscal conditions allow.
An immediate scrapping of NI for that age group would cost £5.1bn, according to the Resolution Foundation.
Under-25s would lose eligibility for the health element of Universal Credit and Pip, and a legal job guarantee would tie benefits to taking up help.
Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the subsidised jobs guarantee would be extended to 18-24-year-olds on Universal Credit after 12 months, helping over 90,000 people by March 2029.
The Conservatives, through Helen Whately, want employer NI halved, while Milburn backed slowing the convergence of youth minimum wage rates.

stories.headline: Britain could face Ireland genocide claim under new definition
stories.claim: UK experts warn a looser ICJ definition of genocide could expose Britain to legal claims, ahead of a Rohingya ruling this week.
stories.summary: Britain could face genocide claims over its past and present conduct, from the Irish potato famine to Kenya's Mau Mau suppression, if the International Court of Justice loosens the legal test for genocide. A Policy Exchange report published on Sunday, written with former ambassador Sir John Jenkins, international lawyer Dr Tom Grant and Air Marshal Edward Stringer, warns that a lower bar could let adversaries seek rulings against British ministers, officials and military alliances. The ICJ is due to rule this week on whether Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya amounts to genocide, and some states and campaign groups are pressing for the threshold to be lowered to a 'reasonable inference' of intent. The current standard, applied in cases such as Srebrenica, requires that genocidal intent be the only reasonable explanation for a state's conduct. The report also includes forewords from former Ukrainian foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba and Aharon Barak, who argue that intent must remain a high bar.

stories.headline: Vulcan rocket fails on first Amazon Leo launch, losing 40 satellites and likely grounding rocket
stories.claim: ULA's Vulcan rocket failed on Sunday, losing 40 Amazon Leo satellites, and is expected to be grounded indefinitely.
stories.summary: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed about ten minutes into its Sunday launch from Cape Canaveral, losing 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. It was the first total mission failure for ULA since it was formed in 2006. The rocket was a custom six-booster Vulcan with a Centaur V upper stage built for low Earth orbit, and the boosters and fairing separated normally before the anomaly. Sources told Ars Technica the fault lay in the booster stage, which kept burning for at least 30 seconds past its planned shutdown, and the Centaur upper stage then tried to correct the spin. ULA says it will investigate the cause and provide updates, and the rocket is expected to be grounded for an indefinite period. The setback hits Amazon's plans to challenge SpaceX's Starlink with its Leo network, which has 396 satellites in orbit against a planned 3,292. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches booked, and the grounding threatens US Space Force launches and NASA's Artemis programme. The next mission, LV-02, was due within weeks and is probably on hold.

stories.headline: Global banks set to enter 2027 on strong footing, Moody's report says
stories.claim: Moody's says global banks enter 2027 on a strong footing, with a stable outlook for the sector.
stories.summary: Global banks are set to start 2027 in a strong position, according to a Moody's Ratings report published on Monday. The agency said lenders have adapted to shifting markets and absorbed sudden shocks during a rapid monetary tightening cycle, leaving them better placed to handle geopolitical and economic uncertainty. Moody's has assigned a "stable" outlook to global banks for 2027, meaning it expects credit fundamentals in the sector to hold steady over the next 12 months. The view signals confidence in bank profitability and balance sheets heading into the new year. Because the report covers banks worldwide, it is a useful gauge for investors watching lenders' credit quality.

stories.headline: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
stories.claim: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, founder of the Guadalajara Cartel, has died in hospital aged 80.
stories.summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, one of the most notorious drug traffickers in history, has died in hospital in Guadalajara aged 80. Known as the "Boss of Bosses", he led the Guadalajara Cartel, which dominated Mexican drug smuggling during the 1980s cocaine boom. He forged the alliance with Colombian cartels, including Pablo Escobar's Medellin Cartel, that moved cocaine into the United States. He was captured in 1989 and had been in state custody since, and was granted house arrest in 2022 but was never transferred because of ankle-monitor problems. His organisation later split, giving rise to the Sinaloa Cartel led by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. His death closes a chapter in the history of the drug trade.

stories.claim: Canadian PM Mark Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese, European or Japanese carmakers if US trade talks fail to protect the auto sector.
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned that Ottawa could look to Chinese, European or Japanese carmakers if trade talks with Washington fail to protect an integrated North American auto industry. Speaking in Phnom Penh on Monday, he said the continental market has become less integrated because of US trade actions, and he stressed that talks with the US remain his priority. stories.headline: South Korea to inspect all exam takers' glasses after top tax scorer confesses to AI-assisted cheating
stories.claim: South Korea will inspect the glasses of all exam takers after the top scorer on a national tax accountancy exam confessed to AI-assisted cheating.
stories.summary: South Korean authorities plan to inspect the glasses of every exam taker after the country's top tax accountancy exam scorer confessed to cheating with AI. Han Won-seok, 34, said in a video posted on his lawyer's YouTube account on Sunday that he used a miniature camera, a mobile phone and generative AI tools, photographing exam questions, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on his phone. He said he cheated in both rounds of the exam, held in April and July, and he had scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round, missing only one of 160 questions, which had triggered online suspicion. He has submitted a written confession to Seoul police, and the case has been assigned to investigators. The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting, and the government says anyone found to have used AI will lose their qualification and be barred from retaking the test for five years. The scandal comes days before the national college entrance exam, where concern over AI-enabled glasses has already grown, and the government has promised tighter anti-cheating measures.

stories.claim: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have withdrawn from the Bab al-Mandab area, leaving the Houthis in control of the Red Sea strait gateway.
stories.summary: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, including the Southern Armed Forces, have pulled out of the area overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Dhubab Airport, leaving the Iran-backed Houthis in control of the key Red Sea gateway. Yemen's military said on Sunday the troops were being redeployed to defend Aden, the interim capital, which the Houthis have repeatedly attacked. The Houthis seized the area in a surprise offensive in September, and the withdrawal ends a weeks-long counter-offensive to retake it. Houthi-run media say they now control the evacuated ground, while Saudi Arabia has not commented. The strait matters because Saudi Arabia has relied on Red Sea oil exports since the US and Israeli war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, and the seizure has pushed up global oil prices. The Houthis say they will not target shipping generally but will keep attacking vessels from Saudi Arabia. The UN estimates about 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, with hundreds killed.

stories.headline: Ousted Bangladesh PM Hasina says she will return home in December despite death sentence
stories.claim: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December despite a death sentence handed down in absentia.
stories.summary: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister, has told AFP she will return home in December, saying 'no threat of death' will keep her away. Speaking by email from India, where she has been in hiding since fleeing in August 2024, the 79-year-old said she had made up her mind and was already preparing the trip, and her lawyers have applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national ID card through the high commission in New Delhi. A Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia in 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to a crackdown on student protesters. Dhaka says she has no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal, that she would face execution if she returns, and it has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review. Hasina rejected the trial as illegitimate, denied that her Awami League was behind recent petrol bomb attacks, and said she faces more than 600 false cases and would not ask India for help to return. Analysts read the pledge as an effort to keep the banned Awami League relevant to its supporters, and it raises the risk of a fresh flashpoint between Dhaka and New Delhi.

stories.headline: Apple launches Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking 200,000 US participants
stories.claim: Apple has launched a Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking up to 200,000 US adults to rate AI health answers.
stories.summary: Apple has launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, a research programme run with the clinical AI platform OpenEvidence that asks members of the public to test AI health answers. Enrolment opened on Sunday through a new iOS app, and Apple is recruiting up to 200,000 participants. Those eligible must live in the US, be 21 or older and own an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or newer. Participants ask text-based health questions and rate the answers for accuracy, detail and relevance; the answers draw on peer-reviewed sources such as the New England Journal of Medicine and JAMA. The app does not use Siri or Apple Intelligence. Users may optionally share HealthKit data such as activity, sleep and lab results, and Apple says participant data stays confidential and will not be used to train AI models, though it may inform feature development. Participation can last up to 12 months, with surveys included. The study comes as about one in three US adults already use AI chatbots for health information, and it aims to shape how health AI tools are designed.

stories.headline: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham pledges early intervention and a benefits backstop to tackle youth unemployment, following the Milburn review.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a root-and-branch rethink of support for young people, citing the Milburn review into youth unemployment. The number of Neets, 18- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training, has passed one million for the first time in over a decade. The review promises almost half a million job and education opportunities within ten years, but also recommends a new youth allowance at universal credit's standard rate for some under-25s, ending some PIP and health-element entitlements. It also proposes a five-year cut in employer National Insurance for 21 to 24-year-olds, which the Resolution Foundation estimates could cost up to £5bn. Opposition parties have criticised the plans, with Labour calling cuts to child disability payments a charter for human misery. Burnham's government is also guaranteeing a fully funded six-month job after 12 months on universal credit.

stories.claim: Dollar hits 19-month high as Fed Governor Waller signals possible half-point rate hike in December.
stories.summary: The dollar climbed to a 19-month high on Monday after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate rise may be needed in December if October core inflation comes in around 0.3% or higher. A hawkish Fed would support the dollar and weigh on risk-sensitive assets.

According to the complaint, quarterly earnings fell 9%, or about $800m, to $8.1bn as PC demand weakened, while Tan blamed an unprecedented memory crunch that has pushed up PC chip costs as supply shifts to AI data centres. Intel shares have dropped 37.5% over the past month but remain up about 51% for the year, leaving the company's guidance credibility under scrutiny.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage with tower arms for first time after Flight 15
stories.claim: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the tower's chopstick arms at Starbase, the first ship capture after orbit, though the booster was lost.
stories.summary: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the mechanical chopstick arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas on Saturday, the first time a ship has been captured after returning from orbit. The spacecraft, about 170 feet long and travelling at more than 17,000 mph before re-entry, had launched on Friday at 5:47pm Eastern on its 15th test flight. It circled Earth 14 times and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, and SpaceX says its heat shield and other systems performed well. The planned double catch failed because the 33-engine Super Heavy booster reported a guidance and navigation fault, was diverted into a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico and was destroyed there; the cause is under investigation. SpaceX has previously caught boosters on three earlier flights. Experts caution that heat shield and engine readiness for rapid reuse remain unproven, though full reusability could sharply cut launch costs. Musk said on the Q3 earnings call that a successful catch on the next flight was more likely than not, and NASA's Artemis III is targeted for summer 2027.

stories.headline: Australia to receive COVID-19 vaccine within months
stories.claim: UK scientists are developing an Oxford Ebola Bundibugyo vaccine that could reach trials within two to three months.
stories.summary: Oxford scientists are developing an experimental vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which could be ready for clinical trials within two to three months. The outbreak is centred on the Democratic Republic of Congo, with around 750 suspected cases and 177 deaths reported. The WHO raised the risk in the DRC to very high and declared a public health emergency of international concern on Sunday. stories.headline: Gulf conflict energy shock set to drive next wave of food inflation, Rabobank warns
stories.claim: Rabobank warns the Gulf conflict energy shock will push US food inflation to 4-6% by December 2026.
stories.summary: Food prices are set to climb again as the Gulf conflict drives up energy, diesel and fertiliser costs, according to Rabobank, which forecasts US food inflation of 4-6% year on year by December 2026, easing to 3-5% through 2027. The energy shock has been intensifying: Brent crude closed at about $94 a barrel on Friday, up 27% since the conflict began and well above the $63 the UK Office for Budget Responsibility had assumed earlier in the week. The Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed, with Iran not formally closing it, as insurance costs soar and sailors avoid the route. The shock is spreading beyond oil. UK gas reached £1.35 a therm against an assumed 74p, touching £1.70 this week, and the 10-year gilt yield rose from an assumed 4.4% to 4.6%, nearly reaching 4.7%. Banks are repricing mortgages and markets now expect the Bank of England to slow rate cuts. Rabobank argues the cushion that softened the 2021-22 shocks is largely gone, and that lower and middle-income shoppers will trade down, squeezing mid-tier brands the hardest.

Meteorologists say this does not guarantee a harsh winter, but it could increase the chance of cold, dry conditions across parts of the Northern Hemisphere later in the season. Adam Scaife of the Met Office said there have been collapses in November before but never this early in the month. Scientists are still investigating, with possible links to unusually warm Arctic ocean temperatures and an exceptionally strong El Niño developing this year. Such disruptions usually bring cold air into Europe and North America a week or two after the upper-atmosphere change.

stories.headline: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
stories.claim: The ClickFix scam tricks users into pasting malicious code via fake Captcha checks, and is now one of the most common ways to infect computers.
stories.summary: A scam known as ClickFix is becoming one of the most common ways criminals infect people's computers with malware, according to Malwarebytes researcher Chris Fistonich. Instead of the familiar image or letter Captcha, victims are told to press keys such as Windows Key plus R, then Ctrl plus V and Enter. This copies malicious code into the clipboard and runs it on the device. The scam is especially effective during the Christmas shopping season, when people visit unfamiliar small-business websites. Fistonich says people are not prepared for it because they trust Captchas and security software. Advice includes pausing before following any on-screen instructions, using security software that blocks malicious sites, and, if compromised, contacting the bank and changing passwords.

A single Class F share, issued to a Founder LLC owned by its seven co-founders, will carry 50.1% of voting power despite having no economic rights, leaving all Class A public holders with just 49.9% of the vote. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holding Class T stock will elect most of the board, and employees receive Class E shares with limited voting rights. The structure follows Alphabet, Meta and Snap, where founders also hold outsized control. stories.headline: EV makers aren’t counting on Democrats to revive tax credits, CNBC says
stories.claim: EV makers Rivian, Lucid and Scout say they are not counting on Democrats to restore federal EV tax credits.
stories.summary: The chief executives of Rivian, Lucid and Scout Motors say they are not banking on Democrats restoring federal support for electric vehicles. The $7,500 federal tax credit ended for EVs bought after 30 September 2025, and sales have fallen since a pre-deadline spike. Democrats take control of Congress in January after their midterm wins, but their early priorities lie elsewhere, such as healthcare. Rivian's RJ Scaringe said he hoped for middle ground with President Trump but expects difficulty, while Lucid's Silvio Napoli advised planning for the worst. Scout, backed by Volkswagen, says it was designed not to rely on legislation and would prefer support aimed at production costs. The average new EV sold for $55,879 in September, against $50,562 for all new cars, so price remains the key obstacle. California's MyFirstEV rebate offers some help to state-based EV-only makers.
key_points: The $7,500 federal EV tax credit ended for vehicles bought after 30 September 2025.
Rivian, Lucid and Scout say they are not relying on Congress to restore support.
Democrats take control of Congress in January, but their early focus is healthcare and oversight.
The average new EV sold for $55,879 in September, versus $50,562 for all new cars.
California's MyFirstEV rebate waives its price cap for in-state EV-only carmakers such as Rivian and Lucid.
stories.market_take: Lack of federal support keeps EV demand pressured, a modest negative for EV makers that depend on buyer incentives.

stories.headline: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer hit by unauthorized external access
stories.claim: Riken suspended Japan's Fugaku supercomputer after unauthorised external access to its connection system.
stories.summary: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer, one of the world's leading machines, has been temporarily shut down after unauthorised external access to the system used to connect to it. The research institute Riken, which runs Fugaku, announced on 16 November that personal or other user information may have been compromised, though the extent of any leak is not yet known. The incident has been reported to the education ministry, and Riken is investigating which parts of the connection system were affected, for how long, and whether data was actually taken. No date has been given for resuming service. Fugaku, developed with Fujitsu and used by automotive, pharmaceutical and materials firms as well as universities, is central to Japanese research, so a leak of corporate or academic data could hurt the country's industrial competitiveness.

stories.headline: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
stories.claim: Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw North Sea field, approved by the UK government last month.
stories.summary: Gas has started flowing from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, after the UK government gave the project its green light last month. Operator Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Equinor, says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes, or about 2% of total UK demand once imports are included. Gas will be sent to the Shearwater platform and then piped to St Fergus in Aberdeenshire. The government says the 11-year field will add £2.9bn to the economy and protect hundreds of jobs. The start-up has drawn criticism from environmental groups and some Labour backbenchers, while the decision on the larger Rosebank field remains pending.

stories.headline: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 doesn't generate images, it paints them
stories.claim: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 creates photorealistic paintings by simulating individual brushstrokes in code, per an Anthropic engineer.

stories.headline: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
stories.claim: Childlight reports AI-related child sexual abuse material reports rose over 8,400% in two years, from about 4,700 in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025.
stories.summary: Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, according to new research from Edinburgh-based Childlight. AI-related abuse material, including deepfakes made with "nudify" apps, rose from about 4,700 cases in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The data comes from reports filed by tech companies with the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Childlight says better detection may explain part of the jump, but calls it an extraordinary rise. Separately, the Internet Watch Foundation found 6,310 AI images meeting the legal definition of child sexual abuse in the first half of 2026, 40% above last year's total. Childlight estimates over 300 million children worldwide suffer technology-facilitated sexual exploitation each year and calls on governments to treat the problem as a preventable public health emergency.

stories.headline: Samsung Is Discontinuing These Useful Mobile Apps In December
stories.claim: Samsung will remove the Quick Measure and AR Doodle apps from the Galaxy Store on 31 December.
stories.summary: Samsung is withdrawing two augmented reality apps from its Galaxy Store, with the removal set for 31 December. Quick Measure, a virtual ruler for measuring distances and areas, and AR Doodle, which lets users sketch and add 3D effects to photos and videos, will stop receiving new downloads and update support. Existing installs will keep working, but some features may fail, and the apps will not get compatibility updates for future versions of Android-based One UI. Samsung said it may bring them back in the future but has not given a timeline. Users who want the apps need to download them before the end of the year.

stories.headline: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software

stories.headline: Bali’s Moon Gang Hotel Finds New Life Without Starting From Scratch

stories.summary: Sydney studio YSG has converted a deteriorating vacation residence in Ubud, Bali, into Moon Gang, a five-suite hotel reached by a lane too narrow for cars. stories.headline: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
stories.claim: A House of Lords committee says UK ministers are complacent and unprepared for interconnected threats, and urges a national resilience overhaul.
stories.summary: A Lords committee has warned that the UK government is complacent and underprepared for a 'polycrisis' of linked threats, from cyber-attacks and sabotage to extreme weather. The report, written after months of expert hearings, calls for a dedicated cabinet minister, an annual prime ministerial statement on preparedness, and a booklet for every household like those in Denmark and Sweden. It highlights fragile supply chains: about 90% of the world's 6-APA, the basis of penicillin-type antibiotics, comes from China, and the UK has no integrated penicillin facility. Nearly 95% of UK retail food is supplied by nine companies. BT has just two cable repair ships, one of them 35 years old. The Cabinet Office said it would review the recommendations and pointed to its £1bn-plus investment in pandemic security.

stories.headline: A timber bridge leads the way into this Nova Scotia coastal retreat
stories.claim: RHAD Architects completes Bridge House, a cedar-clad timber holiday retreat on Nova Scotia's South Shore reached by a footbridge.
stories.summary: A holiday home on Nova Scotia's South Shore arrives at its front door by a timber footbridge, a deliberate piece of theatre designed to heighten the sense of arrival. Bridge House, by Dartmouth-based RHAD Architects, is set back on its plot so it cannot be seen from the street, and visitors drive along a path to a parking court before crossing the bridge into the first floor. The entry sequence includes a sheltered outdoor area and a mudroom built for heavy Canadian winter gear. The main living spaces, including kitchen and dining, sit on the piano nobile beneath a double-height hall with a glazed front facing the cove, while bedrooms are upstairs linked by an internal bridge. The cedar-clad volume draws on local boathouses and cabins, and the architects frame it as both rooted in the coast's traditions and contemporary in its response to climate.

stories.headline: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis; Hamas confirms
stories.claim: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis in a Khan Younis strike; Hamas confirms his death.

Israel's military and Shin Bet said in a joint statement that they had struck Abu Younis, a senior Hamas military wing figure who helped plan the 7 October 2023 attack. Hamas said he had joined its armed wing in 1991 and called the strike a cowardly assassination, and Gaza's civil defence said it received his body and that two people were wounded. The strike tests the October 2025 US-backed ceasefire, which both sides accuse each other of violating and which has not halted Israeli strikes or secured Hamas disarmament. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have died since the truce took effect, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in the same period. The killing comes as Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains responsible for military operations while rival Gadi Eisenkot negotiates a coalition.

stories.headline: COP31 nations split over keeping 1.5C target as UN says it will be missed
stories.claim: At COP31 in Antalya, negotiators are split over whether the final deal should keep the 1.5C goal, as the UN says crossing it is imminent.
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, are divided over whether to keep the 1.5C warming limit, which the UN said in September is imminent and effectively unavoidable. The world has already warmed about 1.4C above pre-industrial levels. Palau's president Surangel Whipps Jr called 1.5C an existential threat, and frontline states want the final deal to affirm it as the right goal and return to it as soon as possible. According to AFP observers, the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, including Saudi Arabia and India, see room to drop the target, partly fearing pressure to cut emissions without extra finance. Australia, which is chairing the negotiations, has released a summary of negotiating positions as the talks reach their midway point. Outgoing UN chief Antonio Guterres said any overshoot must be as small and brief as possible. Scientists warn that weakening the target could slow the emissions cuts needed to limit floods, heatwaves and coral loss, and Exeter's Pierre Friedlingstein said returning to 1.5C would require a massive, decades-long roll-out of carbon removal.

stories.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing Android users' photos
stories.claim: Italy's data regulator fined Meta €805m (about $887m) over Facebook's Android photo-access feature, and Meta says it will appeal.
stories.summary: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million), its largest penalty ever, for the Facebook Android app's access to users' photos and videos without specific consent. The regulator said about 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the camera-roll gallery suggestions feature, which has run since 2023. It found that a single app-wide permission covered several features and was presented with a vague warning, and it cited Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation. The Garante used ePrivacy rules to sidestep the one-stop-shop system that would normally send the case to Ireland, where Meta's EU base sits, rejecting Meta's argument. Meta must obtain separate consent within 60 days, explain the feature clearly and make it off by default, including for existing users. The fine equals roughly 0.4% of Meta's 2025 turnover of $201bn. Meta says it strongly disagrees, will appeal and argues the permission can be changed at any time. The penalty follows a $25bn New Mexico judgment against the company last month. A separate look at a 2026 cloud feature is planned.
key_points: Italy's Garante fined Meta €805m (about $887m), the largest fine it has ever imposed.
About 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the gallery suggestions feature launched in 2023.
The regulator said a single app-wide permission covered several features, with a vague warning, and cited Meta's lack of cooperation.
Meta has 60 days to obtain separate consent, explain the feature and make it off by default.
Meta strongly disagrees and plans to appeal, arguing the permission can be changed at any time.
The fine is about 0.4% of Meta's $201bn 2025 turnover, following a $25bn New Mexico judgment last month.
stories.market_take: The fine is small relative to Meta's profits, so the direct share price impact is likely minimal.
